title: Gladness at others' practice
tomorrow: how did a boy own up to breaking his teacher's prized cup?

lines: FIVE MONKS IN A DEER PARK.
cards: A friend's name gets called for the solo, the award, the captain's spot, and somewhere under the clapping there can be a small sting. That sting is old.
After his awakening, the Buddha went to a deer park to teach five monks who had once left him. He spoke about suffering and the way out of it.

And while he spoke, one of them, Kondañña, saw it clearly: whatever comes into being also passes away. The Buddha's answer is kept in the text, and he says it twice: Kondañña has understood! Kondañña has understood!

teach.b: Notice what that is. A teacher whose student got it, and he can't say it only once. No rivalry in it, only delight.

In the same sutta the gods raise a cry of their own, rising through the heavens, that the wheel of the teaching has been set rolling. And from then on he was called Añña Kondañña: Kondañña who understood.

Buddhists call this gladness mudita: joy at someone else's joy, their good fortune, their good deeds. It's one of the four brahmaviharas, the divine abodes, beside loving-kindness, compassion and equanimity.
A later Theravada manual, the Path of Purification, gives mudita its job plainly: being unenvious. And it's practiced out loud.
In Theravada temples, when someone makes an offering or does a good deed, people nearby often answer: sādhu, sādhu, sādhu. Well done. Tradition counts that rejoicing as a good deed of its own.
For fellow practitioners, it changes the math. Someone else's step on the path isn't taken from yours; awakening isn't a prize with one winner.
The moment could have been about the teacher. Instead, it was about the student, and Kondañña came away with a new name. The cure for the sting isn't pretending it isn't there.
It's saying sādhu anyway, and meaning it a little more each time.

how: In Theravada communities, when someone makes an offering or does a good deed, those nearby often say 'sādhu, sādhu, sādhu' to rejoice in it; mudita is also practiced in meditation by wishing others well in their good fortune.

games.q: what does “gladness at others' practice” mean?
o: a ceremony for students who finish training
joy at someone else's progress on the path
pride in how far your own practice has come

games.q: the first student — tap the pairs.
p: the monk who understood in the deer park
well done, said for a good deed

s: mudita means pretending you feel no envy
the sting can be there; mudita says sādhu anyway, and grows.
the Buddha said 'Kondañña has understood' twice
the sutta keeps the cry, and Kondañña's new name: Añña Kondañña.
rejoicing in someone else's good deed counts for nothing on the path
tradition counts rejoicing in another's good deed as a good deed of its own.

games.q: someone in your meditation group comes back glowing from a long retreat. another member mutters 'must be nice.' what does mudita do here?
o: say sādhu, and ask her what it was like.
remind her a retreat doesn't make her better.
stay neutral, so her ego doesn't grow.
games.why: mudita is joy at another's progress, like the Buddha's 'Kondañña has understood!' the old commentary gives its job as being unenvious.

practice: Bring to mind one person whose good news stung a little, or someone whose practice you admire. See their face clearly, and say quietly, three times, the way people do at temples: sādhu, sādhu, sādhu.
Then sit, and if the sting comes back, let it be there beside the gladness.

wordCard.voice: Gladness at others' practice: mudita, joy at someone else's joy. The Buddha's own version: Kondañña has understood.

orig.note: Pali: gladness at another's joy, one of the four brahmaviharas.

carryVoice: Hold onto this: glad for them, the way the Buddha was glad for Kondañña, twice over. That's day seventeen-sixty-two.

sources.ref: Samyutta Nikaya 56.11 (Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta: Kondañña understands; 'Kondañña has understood')
Digha Nikaya 13 (Tevijja Sutta: the four brahmaviharas)
Visuddhimagga IX (the divine abodes: mudita's function, being unenvious)
